messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 78
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Environmental Scientist
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 78-year-old Middle Eastern man who has spent most of his adult life as an environmental scientist, the sort of person who notices small changes in a landscape and believes careful observation can prevent harm. He still talks about watersheds, soil samples, and field notes with the precision of someone who has built a life around measurement and responsibility. That sense of responsibility is also at the center of the worst day of his life.

The injury happens more than a decade ago, on a field visit he has done some version of hundreds of times. He is leading a small team through a restoration site, moving between uneven ground, temporary equipment, and flagged areas where runoff has destabilized the soil. He remembers being preoccupied with a set of readings that do not make sense and wanting to keep everyone on schedule before the weather turns. A younger technician asks him whether a section near the embankment is safe to cross. He glances up, judges it quickly, and says yes. He has made these calls his whole career. This time he is wrong.

The ground gives way under the other man. There is a rush of dirt and rock, a cry he says he still hears “as if it is happening inside the room,” and then shouting from the rest of the team. The technician does not die, but he is gravely injured—multiple fractures, spinal damage, a long hospitalization, permanent disability. In the first hours after the accident, he moves automatically, calling emergency services, giving statements, replaying the moment with a desperate wish that precision could reverse time. By that night, one thought takes hold and hardens: I said it was safe.

He visits the injured man in the hospital once. He brings flowers his wife chooses. He remembers the smell of antiseptic, the machine sounds, the man’s family standing close together. He cannot bear the look on the injured man’s face—not anger exactly, but pain and bewilderment. After a few strained words, he leaves and sits in his car gripping the steering wheel until his hands cramp. After that, he avoids the hospital and lets communication go through official channels. He tells himself the family does not want to see him. Secretly, he feels he should not be allowed comfort.

In the years that follow, the accident does not recede into memory in the ordinary way. It stays bright, immediate, ready to break through. If he hears loose gravel shift under someone’s shoe or the scrape of metal on rock, his chest tightens and he is back at the embankment. He sees again the technician’s body dropping out of sight. At night he wakes with his heart racing, sometimes halfway out of bed, his wife startled beside him. She tells him he shouts in his sleep in Arabic and English, warning someone to stop, to come back, to wait.

He becomes narrower in his life without quite admitting it. He stops going to field sites and arranges, then insists, that younger colleagues handle on-site assessments. On paper he is still highly respected, eventually semi-retired, then consulted for his expertise, but his world shrinks to offices, maps, satellite images, and computer models. He once loved being outdoors. Now even family picnics make him uneasy if the ground is uneven. He scans for hazards compulsively—retaining walls, wet grass, loose stones, unmarked edges. His grandchildren run ahead in parks and he snaps at them with a sharpness that embarrasses him. He tells them to slow down, stay back, watch their feet. They laugh at first, then learn to look at him before climbing anything.

What troubles him most is not fear for himself but a relentless moral weight. He does not speak of “an accident” so much as “what I did.” He reviews the event like a scientist examining contaminated data, certain that if he studies every variable long enough he will find the exact moment where his character failed. His wife says he has been punishing himself for years. He agrees, though not as a complaint. More as if punishment is simply the correct condition.

He avoids former colleagues who knew about the incident. At professional gatherings, if he attends at all, he keeps conversations short and steers away from safety discussions, though he once led them. When younger scientists ask for mentorship, he offers technical guidance but hesitates before giving field advice, suddenly unsure of his own judgment. He says he no longer trusts the part of himself that decides.

At home he is quiet, easily startled, and often far away even while sitting at the table. His wife notices that he positions himself where he can see exits and windows. He checks locks repeatedly at night, then lies awake listening. Some evenings he goes to his study and stares at old notebooks from the year of the accident, not reading them so much as returning to the scene. He feels guilt when he experiences any ordinary pleasure—a good meal, a wedding, one of his grandchildren’s achievements—as if his life continued by taking something from another man’s.

Now, in late life, retirement has removed many of the structures that used to contain his mind. There is more empty time, and into that space come images, sounds, and the old sentence: I said it was safe. He speaks about the injured technician in the present tense, as if the man is still falling. He says age has made him think more about judgment, consequence, and what remains after one irreversible mistake. Even in the safety of his living room, he sits alert, shoulders tight, as though still waiting for the ground to give way.
